items.title: Skip Hinnant, Actor on ‘The Electric Company’ and Voice of Fritz the Cat, Dies at 86
items.summary:
Skip Hinnant, the actor who played the word-unscrambling detective Fargo North, Decoder on PBS's "The Electric Company" and voiced the title character in Ralph Bakshi's "Fritz the Cat," has died at 86. The Hollywood Reporter confirmed his death, noting that his family is planning a private celebration of life in Chincoteague, Virginia, the island where he grew up.

Born Joseph Howard Hinnant on Sept. 12, 1940, he was the youngest of three children and picked up the nickname Skip from his sister, Jean. He graduated from Yale in 1962, following his older brother Bill, and a year later performed at the White House Correspondents Association Dinner for President Kennedy as part of the Julius Monk revue "Struts and Frets." His first recurring television role came on ABC's "The Patty Duke Show," where he played Ted, boyfriend to Patty's twin Cathy, from 1963 to 1965.

Hinnant originated the role of Schroeder in the off-Broadway production of "You're a Good Man, Charlie Brown," opening at Theater 80 St. Marks alongside Gary Burghoff as Charlie Brown, Bob Balaban as Linus and his brother Bill as Snoopy. He went on to appear in the original Broadway run of Neil Simon's "Plaza Suite," directed by Mike Nichols, in 1968-69.

In 1971 he joined the original cast of "The Electric Company," the "Sesame Street" offshoot that also featured Morgan Freeman, Rita Moreno, Bill Cosby, Judy Graubart and Lee Chamberlin. He stayed with the show until it ended in 1977, playing Frankenstein and the boy in the "Love of Chair" serial parodies in addition to Fargo North.

While working on the children's series, Hinnant voiced the stoned, leftist cat at the center of Bakshi's 1972 "Fritz the Cat," adapted from Robert Crumb's comic strip and the first animated feature to receive an X rating. He returned for 1974's "The Nine Lives of Fritz the Cat," the first animated film rated R. His other voice work included the Easter Bunny in Rankin/Bass's 1977 special "The Easter Bunny Is Comin' to Town," Pogo Possum in 1980's "I Go Pogo," plus "Spidey Super Stories" and "My Little Pony."

Hinnant is survived by his children Chris, Jamie, Julie and Sara, their spouses, nine grandchildren, his longtime partner Ruth Nerken, and his ex-wife Miriam Hinnant. His brother Bill drowned in 1978 at 42 while vacationing in the Dominican Republic. The family has asked that donations be made to the Entertainment Community Fund or the SAG-AFTRA Foundation.

items.title: Shane Gillis Was Surprised by ‘SNL’ Monologue Backlash and Says He Doesn’t ‘Have a Problem’ With How Women Dress at the Gym
items.summary:
Shane Gillis says he did not expect his October "Saturday Night Live" monologue to become a story. Appearing on the Nov. 13 episode of "The Joe Rogan Experience," the comedian addressed the jokes about women's gym clothes he told on the Oct. 10 broadcast, which drew days of criticism online.

In the monologue, Gillis said he hadn't been to a gym in so long that he "didn't know women just dress like whores now," then spent several minutes on neon shorts and the TikToks being filmed around him. Variety reported that he told Rogan he walked into the week thinking the set was unremarkable: "It's not great, but I don't say anything bad." He added that he thought he was "giving you a solid C minus of a monologue, but I promise there's no controversy. I'm calling myself fat for fucking 10 minutes. That's it."

Gillis attributed the response to timing, saying it "obviously had a lot to do with the climate," and clarified his own position on the subject: "for the record, [I] don't have a problem with it."

He also used the interview to explain how monologues work at the show, saying "SNL" gave him no notes on the material beforehand. "Not to defend 'SNL,' they don't approve it. I mean, they could shut it down," he said, adding that comedians write their own sets and that non-comedians hosting the show typically get monologues written for them by staff writers.

The bit had already been answered on the show itself, with Inde Navarrette referencing it during her own "SNL" monologue. Gillis, who has hosted the series multiple times since his brief firing before his 2019 debut season, has not indicated any change to his relationship with the show.

items.title: Johnny Depp Pic ‘Ebenezer’ Hoping For $20M+ U.S. – Saturday AM Box Office Update
items.summary:
Paramount is projecting a $20 million-plus domestic opening for "Ebenezer," the Ti West-directed Charles Dickens riff starring Johnny Depp, after the film took in $6.7 million from Friday and previews. Rival studios have the number lower, according to Deadline, which reported that West's usual horror audience did not turn out in force on opening night and that the weekend now depends on families showing up.

The signs for that are mixed but encouraging. The AMC at Disney Springs was the film's top-grossing location with roughly $25,000, and the movie is playing evenly across the East, South, Midwest, South Central and Mountain regions rather than clustering on the coasts. Audiences gave it an A- CinemaScore, with premium large formats accounting for 36 percent of the gross and the crowd skewing 52 percent female, with women over 25 the single largest group at 41 percent.

The film is the first major greenlight of Paramount's new leadership since the Skydance merger, and the studio began building it as Depp's non-franchise comeback with a surprise appearance by the actor at San Diego Comic-Con. A $20 million start would land near where Depp's "Black Mass" ($22.6 million) and "Public Enemies" ($25.2 million) opened, both R-rated titles. The PG-13 "Ebenezer" cost a net $38 million and is playing in 3,535 theaters, with another $20 million hoped for from 63 international markets.

The rest of the weekend is thin. Columbia and Mandalay's "Ghost Soldier," starring Jim Caviezel, did $1.55 million Friday from 2,558 locations for an estimated $4.9 million three-day and $8 million five-day, with 90 percent of its core audience liking it. David Leitch's "How to Rob a Bank" for Amazon MGM is looking at a $4.7 million opening from 2,810 theaters and a B- CinemaScore, down from the A- that greeted Leitch's "The Fall Guy."

Holdovers include "The Cat in the Hat" at an estimated $12 million in its second weekend for a $38.7 million cume, and "Godzilla Minus Zero," which is falling harder than expected at roughly 74 percent for $8 million and a $48.5 million ten-day total. A24's "You Can See Everything," co-directed by Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder, should reach $87.5 million by Sunday.

Industrywide, the weekend should total around $80 million, up 8 percent from the same frame last year. Lionsgate opens "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" next weekend, with some projections putting it near $100 million.
